minutes.headline: Task force leaned toward flat residential fee, tiered commercial fee, and asked for more tiers for large properties.
minutes.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a revised consultant document on a proposed stormwater utility fee. Members compared property counts, tested revenue totals against a roughly one million dollar target with Chapter 90, and worked through how big commercial properties and large apartment complexes should be tiered. They compiled follow-up questions for the consultant, approved last month's minutes, and heard an update on library stormwater improvements.

budget_items.what_was_said: Members recalled the original budget target was over a million, and the fee scenarios would fall a bit short, with some covered by Chapter 90.
Single and multifamily residential were settled as tier one at the per-year fee.

budget_items.what_was_said: Table figures for residential properties at the per-property rate, plus a multifamily sum, were read out.
Non-residential tier four sum was read as the largest line.
The staff member described drainage budget, a carried balance, and assumed Chapter 90 at the 10-year average, with possible increase from a bond uncertain.
A one-ton dump truck and other equipment purchases were discussed, to be spread over several years rather than one outlay.
If treated as individual units or tier ten, the complex would add roughly ten thousand dollars or more to totals.
A comparison town charges tiered flat fees by impervious area with a cap.
Billing via property tax bills was favored, with an admin position and mailing costs part of the utility budget.

decisions.decision: Members present favored alternative one for single and multifamily residential and alternative four for non-residential, provided large complexes land in higher tiers.
Members agreed to ask for added tiers (tier 11, possibly 12) at the upper end to capture very large properties like the Walmart plaza.

Questions for the consultant agreed: what is in the vacant category and whether it has impervious area, where the Arrive complex falls, the five tier-10 properties and their impervious area, and condo treatment; questions to be circulated to members before sending.
A member agreed to ask the consultant for property lists for tiers five to ten and confirm Arrive's classification.
Credits/waivers for on-site stormwater mitigation were deferred, possibly to revisit around year three.
The next meeting, the last before town meeting, will review a draft and what will be presented to residents; Bill said he would put something together.
A spreadsheet adding residential, multifamily, commercial and Chapter 90 income was to be built.

what_happened.line: Members present favored one residential fee level for single and multifamily homes and a tiered non-residential fee, if large complexes land in higher tiers.
Members agreed to ask the consultant for added top tiers, 11 and possibly 12, to capture very large properties such as the Walmart plaza.
A list of questions for the consultant was agreed, covering the vacant category, where the Arrive complex falls, tier-10 properties and condo treatment; it will be circulated first.
Credits or waivers for on-site stormwater mitigation were deferred, possibly to revisit around year three.
Members recalled the revenue target was over a million dollars and the fee scenarios would fall somewhat short, with part covered by Chapter 90.

why_it_matters: A stormwater utility fee would appear as a new charge on property tax bills, and how large commercial properties and apartment complexes are tiered decides how much of the cost falls on them rather than on single-family homes.

No fee has been set: the task force is still gathering consultant data, and the fee scenarios as discussed do not fully reach the revenue target, so the gap would fall to Chapter 90 road funds or other sources.
